text:
## Observations

1. At rotation zero, the sequence is the original array. When scanning from left to right, each element adds one inversion for every strictly greater element already seen.
2. From rotation \(k\) to \(k+1\), exactly the entries with original value \(M-1-k\) wrap from \(M-1\) to zero. Only pairs with exactly one wrapping entry can change their inversion status.
3. A wrapping entry at one-based position \(i\) gains one inversion with each earlier nonwrapping entry and loses one with each later nonwrapping entry. For every pair of wrapping entries, including the pair in both position counts would give a gain and a loss that cancel.
4. Each transition uses the net change for one original value, in descending order from \(M-1\) to \(1\). A value absent from the array has a net change of zero.

## Solution sketch

> At rotation zero, the sequence is the original array. When scanning from left to right, each element adds one inversion for every strictly greater element already seen.

1. Compute the initial inversion count with a Fenwick tree of frequencies indexed by value. For each element, subtract the number of previously seen values less than or equal to it from the total number previously seen, add the difference to the inversion count, and insert the current value. Using an inclusive prefix query keeps equal values from contributing inversions.

> From rotation \(k\) to \(k+1\), exactly the entries with original value \(M-1-k\) wrap from \(M-1\) to zero. Only pairs with exactly one wrapping entry can change their inversion status.

2. Allocate a zero-initialized array of \(M\) inversion changes, indexed by original value. All occurrences of a value wrap together, so their contributions belong in the same array entry.

> A wrapping entry at one-based position \(i\) gains one inversion with each earlier nonwrapping entry and loses one with each later nonwrapping entry. For every pair of wrapping entries, including the pair in both position counts would give a gain and a loss that cancel.

3. During the initial scan, add \((i-1)-(N-i)=2i-N-1\) to the change for \(A_i\). This counts all positions on either side of \(i\). Because the contributions from pairs within the wrapping group cancel, the sum for \(A_i\) is the exact change when that group wraps.

> Each transition uses the net change for one original value, in descending order from \(M-1\) to \(1\). A value absent from the array has a net change of zero.

4. Print the initial count, then visit values from \(M-1\) down to \(1\), adding each stored change and printing the updated count. This emits exactly \(M\) lines. For \(M=1\), only the initial count is printed. For \(N=1\) or an all-equal array, every answer is zero. The algorithm takes \(O(N\log(M+1)+M)\) time and uses \(O(M)\) auxiliary space beyond the input when answers are emitted as they are computed.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
